title: Plane Waves
short_intro: A plane wave is a wave of constant frequency whose wavefronts are infinite parallel planes normal to the direction of travel. Its physical description relies on solving the linear wave equation in three dimensions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic wave kinematics, phase velocity, wavelength, frequency, relation between particle velocity and wave velocity in transverse waves, intensity and energy density.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of the 3D wave equation from Maxwell's equations or elastic continuum, complex wave representation, acoustic impedance, energy flux vector, and boundary conditions for plane waves.

prerequisites: Partial differential equations and chain rule

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Wavefront Geometry
bullets: Wavefronts are flat, parallel planes perpendicular to the propagation vector k.
All points on a given plane share the identical phase at any instant of time t.
Amplitude and phase remain constant across any plane perpendicular to the direction of motion.

concept_notes.heading: Mathematical Representation
bullets: Displacement is expressed as y(x,t) = A sin(kx - omega t + phi) in one dimension.
In three dimensions, the spatial phase term kx is replaced by the dot product k·r.
The wave vector k has a magnitude equal to 2π/λ and points in the direction of propagation.

concept_notes.heading: Particle Velocity versus Wave Velocity
bullets: Wave velocity (v = omega/k) is the speed at which the phase propagates through the medium.
Particle velocity (v_p = partial y/partial t) is the instantaneous transverse speed of a medium element.
The maximum particle velocity is given by v_{p,max} = Aomega, which can exceed wave velocity depending on amplitude.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Transport and Intensity
bullets:
Energy density (E) in a plane wave is the sum of kinetic and potential energy densities, equal to 2pi^2 m' A^2 
u^2.
Intensity (I) is defined as the average power transmitted per unit area normal to the wave vector.

Intensity is directly proportional to the square of the wave amplitude (I propto A^2) and square of frequency (
u^2).

Divide by T dx and take the limit as dx 	o 0 to obtain  rac{partial^2 y}{partial x^2} =  rac{mu}{T}  rac{partial^2 y}{partial t^2}.

derivations.title: Relation between Particle Velocity and Wave Velocity
derivations.conditions: Harmonic plane progressive wave y(x,t) = A sin(kx - omega t)
steps: Differentiate the displacement equation with respect to time t to find particle velocity: v_p =  rac{partial y}{partial t} = -Aomega cos(kx - omega t).
Differentiate the displacement equation with respect to space x to find spatial gradient:  rac{partial y}{partial x} = kA cos(kx - omega t).
Compare the two expressions by noting that Aomega cos(kx - omega t) = -v (kA cos(kx - omega t)) since v = omega/k.

solved_numericals.question: A plane progressive wave is represented by y = 0.05 sin(100pi t - 2pi x), where x and y are in meters and t in seconds. Calculate the frequency and wavelength of the wave.
solution_steps: Compare the given equation y = 0.05 sin(100pi t - 2pi x) with the standard form y = A sin(omega t - kx).

Equate angular frequency: omega = 100pi. Since omega = 2pi
u, we get 2pi
u = 100pi implies 
u = 50 \text{ Hz}.
Equate wave number: k = 2pi. Since k = 2pi/lambda, we get 2pi/lambda = 2pi implies lambda = 1 \text{ m}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string of length 2 m and total mass 0.04 kg under a tension of 16 N.
solution_steps: Calculate the mass per unit length (mu): mu = M / L = 0.04 \text{ kg} / 2 \text{ m} = 0.02 \text{ kg/m}.
Substitute the values of tension T = 16 N and mu into the formula v = sqrt{T/mu}.
v = sqrt{16 / 0.02} = sqrt{800} = 20sqrt{2} \text{ m/s} approx 28.28 \text{ m/s}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The medium is assumed to be infinite, homogeneous, and isotropic unless boundary conditions are explicitly introduced.
Displacements are assumed to be infinitesimally small so that linear wave equations hold true without nonlinear acoustic effects.
Attenuation and absorption losses due to viscosity and thermal conduction are neglected in ideal plane wave formulations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particles of the medium travel along with the plane wave from one point to another.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only energy and momentum propagate forward; individual medium particles oscillate about their equilibrium positions.
common_misconceptions.why: Wave motion is a propagation of state and disturbance, not bulk transport of matter.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particle velocity and wave velocity are the same physical quantity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Wave velocity is the speed of phase propagation, whereas particle velocity is the instantaneous vibrational speed of a mass element.
common_misconceptions.why: Wave velocity depends on elastic and inertial properties of the medium, while particle velocity depends on wave amplitude and time.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The amplitude of an ideal plane wave decreases with distance from the source.
common_misconceptions.correct: An ideal plane wave maintains constant amplitude in all parallel planes as it propagates through a lossless medium.
common_misconceptions.why: Spherical and cylindrical waves experience geometric attenuation (1/r or 1/sqrt{r}), whereas plane waves do not spread out geometrically.

quick_revision: Plane wave wavefronts are infinite parallel planes perpendicular to the wave vector k.
The fundamental wave equation is partial^2 y / partial x^2 = (1/v^2) partial^2 y / partial t^2.

Phase velocity is given by v = omega/k = 
ulambda.
Maximum particle velocity equals Aomega, which is generally different from wave speed v.

Intensity of a plane progressive wave is proportional to A^2 and 
u^2.
